evidence.source: 漢語多功能字庫 (CUHK Multi-function Chinese Character Database)
evidence.text: Analyzes 您 as 心 (semantic) + 你 (phonetic), used as a second-person pronoun. It cites Jin 董解元《西廂記諸宮調》卷五 using 您 in “您且聽着”; Yuan 白樸《梧桐雨》 uses it of a group (“您眾軍”). The database separately records modern honorific use with a twentieth-century example.
evidence.kind: character-specific dictionary analysis and quoted attestations
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 - 字頭「您」

evidence.source: 教育部《異體字字典》 (Taiwan Ministry of Education)
evidence.text: Says 您 is not recorded in 說文. Gives modern Mandarin nín and defines it as a second-person honorific, also used broadly for plural ‘you’; cites 五代史平話 and Yuan 張國賓《合汗衫》 examples. This supports the historical lexicographic record and usage examples, but does not explain the graph's ancient formation.
evidence.title: [A01365] 您 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: “‘您’来了：‘您’作为现代汉语普通话第二人称敬称成因新释” (ResearchGate-hosted article text)
evidence.field: historical corpus search and review of previous proposals
evidence.text: The article reports that searches of CCL, BCC, and Academia Sinica corpora found no pronoun use of 您 before Yuan; a Tang/Five Dynasties epitaph occurrence (“并州您管”) is judged a likely textual error and not a pronoun. It reviews competing explanations: contraction of 你們/你每; contraction of 你老; a relation to Buddhist 仁; nasalization or contact proposals; and development of honorific meaning from plural use. It also reports disagreement over when the honorific sense arose, with claims ranging from late Qing to early twentieth century. These are the article's review and corpus-search assertions, not independently verified transcriptions of the underlying corpora here.
evidence.kind: secondary scholarly review and corpus-search report
evidence.title: “您”来了：“您”作为现代汉语普通话第二人称敬称成因新释

evidence.text: Displays 您 U+60A8 kMandarin as nín. Used here to verify the current reading value; this modern metadata does not demonstrate an ancient phonetic relationship.
evidence.kind: Unihan field reproduction / current reading metadata
evidence.title: U+60A8 - 字嗨！

evidence.text: Displays 你 U+4F60 kMandarin as nǐ. This is current reading metadata, not evidence by itself for the character's historical sound role in 您.
evidence.kind: Unihan field reproduction / current reading metadata
evidence.title: Unicode Han Character 'you, second person pronoun' (U+4F60)

evidence.text: Describes 中原音韻 as a Yuan-period rhyme book recording northern opera pronunciation, with 19 rhyme groups including 侵尋 and initials including 泥. The consulted page explains its system, but did not expose a directly inspected 您 entry here; therefore it cannot establish a specific historical pronunciation for 您 or 你 in this answer.
evidence.title: 中原音韻 - 韻典網

evidence.text: Unicode describes kMandarin as the customary Mandarin reading property and notes it is derived from other Unihan reading fields with corrections. This clarifies the scope of the modern reading metadata.

search_audit.outcome: Unicode GetUnihanData pages were attempted but inaccessible through the browser; ZIP rejected due to unsupported content type. Inspected Ytenx and official MOE description for 中原音韻. No character-specific historical pronunciation entry was directly verified.

Found and inspected current reading values reproduced from Unihan: 您 nín and 你 nǐ. Official character-specific Unicode CGI pages remained inaccessible; the required official click-through URL is therefore unverified.

gaps: Official Unicode Unihan character pages https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=60A8 and https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=4F60 were actually attempted but not accessible in the browser. Current readings were cross-checked in third-party pages; the prompt-provided local row for 您 is nín, but the local file line search yielded no matching rows in this checkout. The official Unicode click-through evidence requirement is unmet.

The exact kMandarin row for 你 was not available from the supplied local row and was not found in the tracked HSK extract; nǐ is externally corroborated by a third-party Unihan data page. Neither modern reading proves a historical sound relationship.

The exact earliest surviving 您 graph form, manuscript witness, and dated occurrence were not inspected. The sources consulted report Yuan-era attestations; the purported Tang/Five Dynasties instance is reported as a likely corruption and non-pronominal, not independently checked against the inscription or editions.

No independently verified Middle Chinese or Baxter–Sagart reconstructions for 您 and 你 were obtained. A reported hypothesis that 心 could cue an older final nasal is not sufficient evidence here to establish historical sound values; no local Baxter–Sagart rows were supplied or inspected.

The specific lexical derivation of the early pronoun remains unsettled: plural contraction (你們/你每), 你老 contraction, nasalization/contact, and Buddhist 仁 proposals have different evidential bases. The reviewed material does not establish one conclusively.

The transition from the early second-person pronoun, including plural use, to the modern honorific is not securely dated. Published claims summarized in the reviewed article differ; the Jin/Yuan examples establish earlier non-honorific or plural functions, not a fixed chronology of the honorific extension.
No original paleographic forms or glyph images for 您 were visually inspected. The character-specific sources accessed do not provide an independently examined sequence of graphic changes.
